title: Closed-Loop Dual-Reference Guidance for Accent Control in Cross-Lingual Voice Cloning
abstract: ntrol in Cross-Lingual Voice Cloning Yuanzhong Zheng, Wei Huang, Ming Ma, Kailun Jin, Youhai Jiang Zero-shot cross-lingual voice cloning often carries the reference speaker's accent into the target language. We propose closed-loop dual-reference guidance, which pairs the original reference with a reusable native anchor constructed by voice conversion (VC). The references initialize separate language-model (LM) states that guide a shared acoustic trajectory; each completed patch then updates both states, keeping their generated histories aligned with the emitted speech. Anchor construction runs once per speaker, and online synthesis uses a frozen TTS model without per-utterance VC. On 20 held-out French speakers, the fixed setting $\lambda^{\!*}=0.33$ reduces residual French LID mass by 73% versus direct cloning, at an ECAPA similarity cost of only $0.042$; relative to anchor-only cloning, it recovers $0.155$. The method achieves the lowest mean WER ($0.009$) and highest mean GOP ($4.750$) among the held-out test arms. In blinded preference tests, native-English listeners favor it over direct cloning on pronunciation naturalness, and over both anchor-only cloning and a TTS$\to$VC cascade on speaker identity. Online RTF is approximately 26% lower than the cascade's ($0.59$ vs. $0.80$), and the same setting reduces Spanish LID mass by 56% without re-tuning. title: ShlokaDhara: A Multi-Speaker Sanskrit Speech Corpus for Learning Meter-Aware Prosody in Text-to-Recitation
abstract: hlokaDhara: A Multi-Speaker Sanskrit Speech Corpus for Learning Meter-Aware Prosody in Text-to-Recitation Harshal Kausadikar, Onkar Kishor Susladkar, Prathmesh Santosh Choudhari, Vedangi Deepak Deshpande, Ismini Lourentzou, Sparsh Mittal Sanskrit verse recitation is governed by $\textit{Chandas}$, a strict prosodic framework defined by rhythmic $\textit{Laghu}$ (light) and $\textit{Guru}$ (heavy) syllables. Because existing Sanskrit speech datasets prioritize ASR or conversational TTS, they lack the metrical fidelity required for authentic verse synthesis. We introduce $\textbf{$\textit{ShlokaDhara}$}$, a 43-hour, multi-speaker Sanskrit speech corpus capturing diverse meters, recitation styles, and melodic variations. We specifically focus on $\textit{Text-to-Recite}$, a synthesis task explicitly requiring both prosodic accuracy and metrical correctness. Benchmarking state-of-the-art TTS architectures via an automated UTMOS (neural MOS) predictor demonstrates that XTTS-v2 achieves the highest perceptual quality. We further validate the XTTS-v2 generated samples using two paradigms: subjective assessments by 16 Sanskrit experts and novel empirical metrics, specifically, syllable-level $\textit{Laghu-Guru}$ duration analysis to objectively quantify structural metrical awareness. Ultimately, this work establishes a robust dataset and evaluation benchmark for prosody-aware computational Sanskrit recitation. title: Speech LLMs That Breathe: Modeling Non-Verbal Vocalizations in Dialogue
abstract: iu, Lixin Zhang, Jiayi Huang, Ziyang Cheng, Yuhao Wang, Ronghua Wu, Qunshan Gu, Yanfeng Wang, Yu Wang The user experience of speech interaction models has improved, benefiting from the modeling of paralinguistic attributes and advances in speech reconstruction paradigms. However, human communication follows extensive norms regarding non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) spanning respiratory, affective, and discourse. The omission of these events imposes inherent limitations on the naturalness of current approaches. In this work, we cover 13 major types of NVVs and construct a natural dialogue dataset that conforms to human conversational norms through an automated synthesis pipeline. We enhance the ability of speech interaction models to generate contextually appropriate NVV events through multi-stage fine-tuning and NVV-aware GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Based on distinct modeling paradigms, we substantially improve the expressiveness of VocalNet and VITA-Qinyu in empathy interactions and role-play dialogues, and further discuss the architectural necessity for achieving high-quality natural speech generation. title: Interpreting SSL Representations for Spoof Detection: a WavLM Study
abstract: llo, Massimiliano Todisco, Nicholas Evans, Anthony Larcher Self-supervised speech models such as WavLM achieve strong spoofing detection performance, yet which layers encode the most spoof-relevant information and what acoustic properties they capture remain opaque. We present a layer-wise interpretability study of WavLM using the ASVspoof 5 database, combining three complementary analyses: (i) per-layer linear probing with attack-level evaluation across speech synthesis, voice conversion, and adversarial attacks; (ii) a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) linking layer representations to spoofing-relevant acoustic features; (iii) an exhaustive grid search over layer subsets showing that use of five layers outperforms full thirteen-layer pooling. CCA analysis reveals that, while most acoustic features peak in alignment with mid-layers and then decay, voice quality measures jitter, shimmer, and the harmonics-to-noise ratio show the opposite trend, with correlation increasing toward later layers. Embedding visualisations reveal that deeper layers capture a continuous acoustic similarity among attacks rather than discrete categories, suggesting these layers encode fundamental synthesis artifacts rather than attack-specific signatures. Comments: 5 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Published at IWBF 2026. title: Too Emotional to Be Fake? Intra-Utterance Emotion Shifts Expose Failure Modes in Speech Deepfake Detectors
abstract: tectors Jingyi Chen, Surya Koppisetti Expressive speech synthesis can now change emotion within a single utterance, yet its impact on deepfake detection remains unclear. We introduce EmoShift, a benchmark comparing emotion-stable (AA) and emotion-changing (AB) speech to examine these effects while accounting for static emotion identity and acoustic confounds. It comprises 7,240 bona fide utterances from four source datasets and 9,720 synthetic utterances generated using four expressive TTS systems. Across seven detectors, we find that emotion changes can make synthetic speech appear more genuine, increasing spoof miss rates by up to 25.3 percentage points on OMG-Emotion at fixed thresholds. Conversely, emotion-changing bona fide speech increases false-alarm rates by up to 24.4 percentage points on IEMOCAP. Further analyses reveal detector-specific sensitivities to emotion trajectories, not fully explained by static emotion identity or splicing artifacts. These findings underscore the importance of emotion dynamics in deepfake detection. Comments: Preprint. title: Noise-Aware Lombard Speech Synthesis via Flow-GRPO for Intelligibility Optimization
abstract: Dingding Yao, Chengzhong Wang, Junfeng Li Voice-based conversational agents are increasingly deployed in real-world settings, where environmental noise often degrades the interactive experience. Therefore, robust acoustic adaptability is essential to maintain natural and intelligible human-computer communication. However, most existing systems remain acoustically insensitive and fail to emulate the human Lombard effect, in which speakers involuntarily adjust their vocal production to preserve intelligibility in the presence of noise. As a result, their communicative reliability degrades under adverse acoustic conditions. To remain intelligible in noisy environments, conversational agents require a mechanism to emulate noise-induced adaptive behavior during synthesis. We propose NIL-TTS, a noise-induced Lombard TTS framework. We integrate a feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) mechanism into a flow-matching backbone for dynamic vocal adaptation. A two-stage training paradigm is utilized: initial supervised fine-tuning on paired Lombard corpora, followed by Flow-GRPO post-training to optimize for intelligibility. Evaluations confirm that NIL-TTS autonomously adjusts its output in response to varying noise conditions, exhibiting key correlates of the human Lombard effect. Driven by these adaptive modulations, the synthesized speech achieves significant intelligibility improvements that scale proportionally with noise intensity. title: Beyond Two Tracks: Speaker-Anchored Full-Duplex Dialogue Recovery
abstract: Chak Sun, Brick Li, Sam Spoken interaction is moving from alternating turns to full-duplex conversation, where an agent listens while speaking. Learning this coordination requires natural dialogue with persistent speaker-resolved tracks, a data requirement that remains difficult to satisfy at scale. Generative recovery offers a route from ordinary recordings, but recovering two voices is not enough: their track assignments can drift as the conversation unfolds. We address this missing link with speaker-anchored routing before diffusion: a 1.84M-parameter module matches the separator's coarse streams to fixed enrollment identities and orders them before a frozen generator reconstructs the speech, without retraining the generator or altering the reconstructed audio. On 25-minute remote conversations, routing cuts wrong-track time from 43.9% to 4.1%, below the 6.2% of matched-enrollment waveform re-identification, with its largest advantage when one participant holds the floor (17.8% versus 28.6%), and raises fixed-track activity F1 from 0.46 to 0.84 while per-chunk reconstruction quality is unchanged. The same router transfers to unseen face-to-face and telephone recordings, and a margin-gated verification step brings their wrong-track time to 0.9-1.7% while embedding 20-36% of the output, where full re-identification embeds all of it. Recovered voices thus become the participant-consistent tracks that full-duplex dialogue modeling needs. Audio examples: this https URL Comments: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. title: Jarvis: Coordination Deserves a Brain of Its Own in Agentic Interactive Models
abstract: o Cai, Zhixian Zhao, Yingda Shen, Yuancheng Wang, Xueyao Zhang, Liqiang Zhang, Teddy Sun, Steve Yves, Zhizheng Wu Interactive models increasingly hand complex reasoning and tool use to a slow brain in the background, leaving a realtime front model free to sustain full-duplex dialogue. Yet the user may refine, cancel or replace a request while its task runs, so a plan or result that made sense a moment ago goes stale. Each new utterance must therefore be read against the work in flight, but the front model follows only the conversation and the back end sees only its own task. Coordination deserves a brain of its own, one that sees both. We introduce Jarvis, a coordination harness where models judge and code enforces. Its typed decision model, JEV, reads each turn against the live tasks and picks among operations built from a versioned task record. Code checks every choice against the current state before applying it, so no decision can act on a task version the user has replaced. Jarvis also rechecks plans before they execute and results before they are spoken, and counts an answer as delivered only once the user has heard it in full. We build two instances of this design. Jarvis-Audio runs unchanged on three full-duplex speech models. Jarvis-Omni adds vision and rechecks the evidence behind an answer before and during playback, since a scene can change while nobody speaks. title: Pearl-Chat: Engineering a native Luganda language model from first principles in JAX and Flax NNX
abstract: JAX and Flax NNX Wesley Kambale, Roland Sankara Autoregressive foundation language models predominantly target high-resource Indo-European languages, imposing computational and morphological penalties on under-represented African languages. Generic multilingual tokenizers routinely exceed fertility rates of 3.2 tokens per word on agglutinative Bantu languages, degrading context efficiency and inflating latency. We present Pearl-Chat, an 8,473,122-parameter ($\sim$8.5M) causal decoder-only transformer engineered for Luganda (Oluganda, ISO 639-2: lg), a low-resource Niger-Congo Bantu language spoken by over 10 million people in East Africa. Built from first mathematical principles in JAX and Flax NNX, Pearl-Chat uses explicit functional state decomposition (this http URL and this http URL), deterministic resumable data streaming via Google Grain, and SPMD tensor parallelism using this http URL. We introduce a byte-level byte-pair encoding (BPE) subword tokenizer trained from scratch on curated Luganda corpora ($V = 8,192$), achieving 4.88 characters per token compression and 1.60 tokens per word fertility, a two-fold compression improvement over LLaMA-3 (128K) and Gemma (256K). The model is trained with a two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 pre-training on 59,501 sequences across parallel, biblical, encyclopedic, and journalistic corpora, and Stage 2 instruction fine-tuning on 510 dialogues with assistant-only loss masking. title: MedSonor: Learning to Use Clinical Audio in Medical LLMs
abstract: cal audio conveys medical information that transcripts may not preserve, but using it in medical responses requires interpreting it alongside clinical requests and dialogue context. Existing medical audio supervision largely targets classification or recognition, while general audio-language models lack specialized medical knowledge and direct feedback for open-ended responses. We present MedSonor, a medical dialogue model integrating medical knowledge, spoken dialogue, and clinical audio understanding. We pair authentic medical audio with clinical requests and combine these audio-integrated dialogues with collected medical audio and synthesized spoken dialogues for supervised fine-tuning, followed by two stages of rubric-guided reinforcement learning. We introduce MedVoice-Dial and MedVoice?AID to evaluate responses within supplied multi-turn medical contexts and to requests involving clinical audio, respectively. Across seven medical benchmarks, MedSonor outperforms the evaluated general-purpose open-weight audio-language baselines and ranks highest in aggregate physician preference evaluation, while broadly retaining general speech capabilities. title: Full-Duplex Interaction with Speech, Expressions and Gestures
abstract: d Gestures Siyin Wang, Wenyi Yu, Terumi Chiba, Xianzhao Chen, Xiaohai Tian, Jun Zhang, Lu Lu, Chao Zhang Human face-to-face conversation requires coordinating speech, gestures and expressions across both speaking and listening. We present ELLSA 2, an end-to-end full-duplex dialogue model that jointly optimizes speech interaction and streaming gesture-expression generation. An autoregressive, chunk-wise synthesizer combines pretrained acoustic features with distinct listening and speaking hidden states from the dialogue backbone and speech synthesizer, enabling continuous non-verbal generation even when the model is verbally silent. To translate dialogue understanding into vivid semantic gestures, we introduce contextual semantic calls and template guidance, separating whether to invoke an available semantic gesture from how to realize it. We also establish a curated data and evaluation pipeline for dialog-aware co-speech gesture generation and investigate reference-based multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as automatic judges. Experiments show that ELLSA 2 remains highly competitive with open-source full-duplex speech interaction models and outperforms cascaded baselines across dialog-aware gesture and expression metrics. Semantic template guidance further significantly improves semantic gesture quality. Strong system-level correlations with human judgments support these reference-based scores as useful preliminary metrics for full-duplex and semantic gesture assessment. title: JAVIS: Joint Audio-Visual Interaction and Streaming for Real-Time Conversational Agents
abstract: Conversational Agents Junseok Ahn, Jaehyun Park, Jeongsoo Choi, Joon Son Chung, Ji-Hoon Kim Human communication is inherently multimodal, conveying intent not only through linguistic and vocal cues but also through visual signals. However, existing conversational systems have mainly focused on text or speech, leaving out the visual feedback that is essential for natural interaction. In this paper, we propose JAVIS, an end-to-end streaming framework for real-time audio-visual conversational agents. Our key idea is to let the voice and the face speak from a single representation. On top of a shared LLM, a Joint Refined Head produces a unified audio-visual representation, which is fed into dedicated streaming branches for speech and face generation. This end-to-end design avoids intermediate bottlenecks, enabling real-time generation while keeping speech and face tightly synchronized. In addition, we present JAVIS-Syn, a 334-hour synthetic corpus designed to address the lack of expressive audio-visual dialogue data, covering emotionally rich multi-turn conversations and assistant-style exchanges. Experiments show that JAVIS achieves approximately 200$\times$ lower initial latency than a strong baseline, while outperforming baselines in lip synchronization and facial expression appropriateness. Comments: 5 pages, 2 figures. title: Towards Efficient Simultaneous Inverse Text Normalization with Pretrained Text-to-Text Language Model and Read-Tag-Write Policy Kiet
abstract: o-Text Language Model and Read-Tag-Write Policy Kiet Anh Hoang, Khanh Le, Bao Nguyen, Linh Pham, Dung Vo, Thai Tran, Mai Nguyen, Tri Nguyen, Vu Le Streaming Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is vital for converting spoken-form outputs from streaming Automatic Speech Recognition into formatted written text. Existing streaming ITN methods rely on hybrid systems combining neural tagging with expert-crafted finite-state transducer rules, limiting scalability across domains and languages. While end-to-end models offer superior scalability by learning directly from data, standard encoder-decoder architectures are inherently non-streaming due to global attention. In this paper, we propose an efficient streaming end-to-end ITN system, adapting a pretrained text-to-text model to leverage its robust linguistic knowledge. To enable streaming, we introduce architectural adaptations, a specialized training strategy, a Read-Tag-Write decoding policy, and inference optimizations. Experiments on Vietnamese datasets show accuracy comparable to non-streaming baselines, outperforming hybrid methods while satisfying real-time latency requirements. title: Speech event detector: Timestamped detection of non-verbal vocalizations and background sounds for rich speech transcription Ayush
abstract: ich speech transcription Ayush Kumar Bar, Promila Ghosh Automatic speech recognition produces words but drops the non-verbal content of a recording: the breaths, coughs, sighs and laughter of the speaker, and the horns, music or barking around them. We describe Speech Event Detector, a 5.8-million-parameter convolutional-Transformer model that outputs probabilities every 40 ms for 54 event classes (20 speaker vocalizations and 34 background sounds), together with post-processing that converts these probabilities into timestamped events and a procedure for merging the events into a Whisper transcript. The model is trained on material drawn from seven public datasets whose labels come in incompatible forms: single detected regions, free-text tags with timestamps, temporally strong ontology labels, symbols embedded in transcripts, isolated recordings and environmental recordings. We unify them using rule-based label mapping, recover timestamps for transcript-embedded labels through CTC forced alignment, locating 6,360 of 8,620 sounds, and combine about 168 hours of real annotated training recordings with synthetic mixtures and augmentation using real background noise. Per-class thresholds for two operating profiles are tuned on real held-out recordings, and performance is estimated using two-fold cross-validation. On whole held-out recordings from four datasets, considering the 48 classes with at least ten held-out events, the sensitive profile detects an average of 49 percent of a class's events, covering 67 percent of all 9,367 events, at a macro precision of 0.30. We present Oído, an inference engine that runs open-vocabulary English speech recognition entirely on an ESP32-S3 (240 MHz dual-core Xtensa LX7, 512 KB of SRAM, 8 MB of PSRAM, 16 MB of flash, no neural accelerator). Oído executes a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model with int8 weights, per-frame dynamic int8 activations and int8 attention on the chip's SIMD instructions, with a schedule designed around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. title: LiveSynth: A Streaming Neural Synthesizer for Instrument Cloning and Text-to-Instrument
abstract: Yejin Kim, Kyogu Lee Recently, generative neural synthesizers have enabled zero-shot instrument cloning from reference recordings and timbre generation from text prompts. However, existing systems generate complete audio segments offline, precluding their use as playable instruments. We present LiveSynth, a streaming neural synthesizer with flexible timbre control and interactive generation capabilities, including zero-shot instrument cloning and text-to-instrument synthesis. A feedback-free causal Transformer conditioned on MIDI events and a CLAP timbre embedding outputs continuous audio latents at 100 Hz, which a causal variational autoencoder decodes into audio. Frame-wise timbre conditioning enables continuous timbre morphing, while MIDI-conditioning dropout enables autonomous continuation from a performed prefix. On the NSynth and Slakh datasets, LiveSynth achieved timbre similarity and spectral reconstruction quality comparable to offline baselines. On an M3 MacBook Air, LiveSynth required 8.8 ms of computation per 10 ms audio frame (an RTF of 0.88) with 10 ms algorithmic latency, enabling real-time interaction with a performer. title: People Making Conversation: Evaluating How Naturally Speech Models Converse
abstract: Bastani, Iman Modarressi A conversational speech model has to decide, at every pause, whether to speak. Existing evaluations test boundary detection, policy adherence, or aggregate statistics, not this decision. We place real-time speech systems at 427 pauses and 482 turn ends from 176 unscripted conversations in Seamless Interaction, give each the conversation so far, and score what it generates against what the person did: whether and how soon it speaks at a pause; its latency, length, and wording at a turn end; and whether it can answer a question about the preceding 30 to 120 seconds. Across six systems, the hosted APIs (GPT Realtime, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Grok Voice) respond at almost every pause whichever endpointer they use; only their latency, about 1 to 4 s with silence-based endpointers and about 8 s with semantic turn detection, decides whether the words land inside the pause. The full-duplex models (PersonaPlex, Moshi) are the only systems that regularly stay silent and the only ones that interrupt within a human reaction time. Hosted systems reply longer than the person. Given the history as text, hosted systems recall 41 to 60% of conversation facts under a Claude Opus 5.5 judge and 19 to 26% under a strict word matcher; hearing it as audio, full-duplex models recall 17 to 22% and 12 to 15%. We release the labels, points, harness, and every output. title: MultiPartyTurnBench: Benchmarking Floor Control in Multi-Party Spoken Dialogue
abstract: h Manocha Full-duplex speech systems must decide when to enter, hold, or relinquish the conversational floor, even as multiple speakers overlap or backchannel without taking it. Existing evaluations study dyadic turn-taking or end-to-end agent behavior, but lack a unified, controlled evaluation of genuine floor transitions against confusable non-events in multi-party settings. We introduce MultiPartyTurnBench (MPTB), a benchmark of 240 synthetically generated, channel-separated conversations spanning two to five speakers and six interaction types. MPTB evaluates two complementary tasks: End-of-Turn (EOT) detection distinguishes genuine turn completion from temporary holds, while Interruption (INT) detection distinguishes successful floor takeovers from non-floor-taking speech. Exact event-conditioned annotations enable causal evaluation using false-positive-constrained recall and signed latency. Across acoustic, semantic, and turn-projection baselines, we find a stark asymmetry: learned systems achieve 82.5-92.6% EOT recall at 4.3-11.8% false-positive rates, while INT detection suffers from missed takeovers or excessive false activations. This asymmetry extends to five full-duplex agents which achieve 86.1-95.8% balanced accuracy on turn entry, yet perform near chance (46.9-54.7%) on selective interruption handling. Gemini-3.8-Live yields to 97.7% of backchannels, whereas MiniCPM-o-4.5 yields to only 1.4% of genuine interruptions. These findings establish selective floor control as a distinct, unresolved challenge for reliable multi-party voice interaction. Comments: Under

title: Full-duplex Spoken Language Modeling with Discrete Diffusion
abstract: Ku, Ankita Pasad, Ante Jukić, Zhehuai Chen, Boris Ginsburg We introduce Diffuplex, a full-duplex spoken language model based on discrete diffusion that achieves an unprecedented balance between linguistic intelligence and response efficiency. With thinking mode, Diffuplex delivers 13.0 tokens per forward pass, reaching an average of 1872 tokens per second and substantially surpassing the frontier autoregressive (AR) models in decoding speed. Without thinking, Diffuplex matches the first-audio latency of existing full-duplex models while achieving markedly stronger linguistic intelligence. This capability is enabled by separating when to say from what to say at the training level, rather than compressing both into a single autoregressive timeline. During inference, Diffuplex continuously tracks the user speech through an AR interaction policy, while independently generating and refining response content through parallel diffusion. Consequently, semantic computation is no longer bounded by the perception audio frame rate, allowing intelligence and responsiveness to improve simultaneously. Taken together, these results establish a new paradigm for spoken agents that can sustain real-time dialogue while devoting parallel computation to intelligent response generation. Training code and checkpoints will be avaliable soon. title: D2: High-Capability Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models from Half-Duplex Backbones Cheng-
abstract: s Cheng-Kuang Chang, Alexander H. Liu, Brian Kingsbury, Hilde Kuehne, Rogerio Feris, Samuel Thomas, James Glass, Kai-Wei Chang Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1. Comments: 17 pages, including references and appendices. title: SCIC: Scope- and Codebook-Aware Instruction Conditioning for Speaker-Adapted Expressive TTS
abstract: Lu, Zongwei Du, Mengtao Xing, Zhuoqun Liu, Zifan Guan, Meiguang Jin, Junfeng Ma Long-form live-streaming TTS requires context-dependent prosody and paragraph-level coherence. However, many existing instruction-based TTS systems use global or uniform conditions, providing limited explicit control over clause-level relative prosodic changes. We introduce Speaker-Relative Inline Prosody Control, where each Pitch, Energy, or Speed instruction targets a clause relative to the preceding clause from the same speaker, while Pause uses an absolute duration interval. In codec-based TTS, Speed and Pause affect sequence length, whereas Pitch and Energy rely on residual codebooks. By analyzing Qwen3-TTS RVQ codebooks, we find that Energy concentrates in early residual codebooks, whereas Pitch accumulates across a deeper prefix. We therefore propose Scope- and Codebook-Aware Instruction Conditioning (SCIC), combining a Temporal Instruction Router for frame-level tag activation with Tag-Specific Codebook Weighting over residual codebooks. SCIC improves speaker-relative Pitch and Energy control over standard instruction fine-tuning using text-token tags. We further apply multi-reward GDPO post-training to jointly optimize control and quality, improving control accuracy while preserving CER and speaker similarity. In long-form synthesis, SCIC produces a more distinct paragraph-level expressive hierarchy than speaker-adapted SFT without instructions. title: HaikuS2S: A Cascaded System For Responding In Verse
abstract: ke, Glenda Tan, Conrad Schaumburg, Shinji Watanabe Expressive speech synthesis has advanced through prosody modeling, yet generating structured poetic speech, such as haiku, remains challenging. Prior work on prosody transfer improves expressiveness, and fine-tuned poetry TTS (text-to-speech) systems capture verse intonation. However, these models do not model haiku's 5-7-5 syllable structure or line-ending pauses. We present a cascaded system, HaikuS2S, combining ASR (automatic speech recognition), LLM (large language model)-generated haiku, and TTS fine-tuning on both prose and custom haiku datasets. Our evaluation focuses on emotion similarity, speech quality, and prosody alignment. In our experiments, we see that our prosody and tonal alignment improve significantly with our fine-tuned systems, particularly the one trained on both general poetry and haiku. We also see that we maintain similar emotion similarity scores across all systems. title: Multi-Dimensional Prosody Judgment For Live Streaming Speech Synthesis
abstract: Zhang, Zhizheng Wu, Meiguang Jin, Junfeng Ma Evaluating live streaming speech synthesis (TTS) requires assessing fine-grained, highly expressive prosody such as emotion, intonation, and energy which traditional MOS predictors fail to capture. While proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) like Gemini can evaluate these aspects, they are too costly for massive inference and reinforcement learning feedback. To address this, we first introduce Live-ProsodyJudge (LPJ), a cost-effective pairwise evaluator distilled from Gemini into Qwen3-Omni. However, we identify a critical flaw in standard multi-dimensional evaluation: verdict coupling. The judge tends to lazily align all individual dimension scores with its overall preference, collapsing a rich multi-dimensional rubric into a single preference bit. To resolve this, we further propose Decoupled-Live-ProsodyJudge (D-LPJ). D-LPJ eliminates the overall verdict target to prevent blind following, masks uncertain pair-dimensions during Supervised Fine-Tuning(SFT), and introduces a novel span-local GRPO strategy that applies normalized advantages strictly to their corresponding rationale spans. Evaluated on highly curated human-annotated test sets, 10 sample balanced-order LPJ achieves higher point accuracy than a single Gemini call, while D-LPJ successfully produces independent,decoupled dimension judgments. Furthermore, in a Best-of-8 TTS candidate selection tournament, the LPJ-selected utterance falls within the human top-3 in 85.29% of high-confidence cases, demonstrating its efficacy for fine-grained TTS preference optimization

title: Alignment-Free Text-Audiobox for Voice Dubbing and Full-Duplex Dialogue Synthesis
abstract: Sanyuan Chen, Min-Jae Hwang, Sho Inoue, Anna Sun, Bokai Yu, David Kant, Dongmin Hyun, Dorian Desblancs, Gregory Antonovsky, Oleg Repin, Peng-Jen Chen, Xutai Ma, Zehai Tu, Juan Pino, Wei-Ning Hsu We present Alignment-Free Text-Audiobox (Text-AB), a unified framework for high-quality voice dubbing and full-duplex dialogue synthesis. Building on a Diffusion Transformer trained with a flow-matching objective, Text-AB departs from the Audiobox system along three dimensions. First, it operates in a latent diffusion framework using DAC-VAE features that encode 48 kHz waveforms into a 25 Hz latent sequence, giving over 10x higher compression than previous EnCodec representations while improving resynthesis quality. Second, Text-AB is alignment-free: it consumes raw text via an off-the-shelf text encoder and learns text-speech alignment through cross-attention, removing the need for forced alignment and explicit duration prediction. Third, we scale model and data substantially, pretraining a 3B-parameter model on 480k hours of monolingual speech, followed by supervised fine-tuning on three downstream tasks: cross-lingual voice dubbing, full-duplex dialogue synthesis, and emotional full-duplex dialogue synthesis. At inference, Text-AB supports one-shot generation for up to ~1 min of speech and arbitrarily long-form generation via a multi-diffusion scheme, plus a multi-stage reranking strategy that enhances quality based on automated metrics. title: Diagnose, Then Refine: A Closed-Loop TTS System with AudioLLM-Guided Correction
abstract: i Liu, Tianrui Wang, Chenglin Xu, Steven Y. Guo, Haizhou Li Current TTS systems typically rely on open-loop, single-pass generation and can produce sporadic local prosodic defects, such as misplaced stress, unnatural pauses, or flattened intonation, that utterance-level metrics often fail to expose. We present LoopTTS, a judge-guided Filter-Judge-Refiner framework for recovering low-quality TTS outputs diagnosed by an AudioLLM. Given an initial utterance from a base TTS model, an AudioLLM Judge identifies salient prosodic issues and generates structured refine instructions; a Refiner, our fine-grained instruction-following TTS model, then performs guided expressive re-synthesis conditioned on the initial utterance, target text, and instruction. To train the Refiner, we construct Refiner-DB, a 42K-example AudioLLM-annotated dataset with word-level prosodic weak supervision. Human evaluation on diagnosed low-quality utterances shows that LoopTTS can detect perceptually salient errors and correct them with the Refiner, outperforming raw generated audio and practical open-loop re-generation baselines in recovery quality. The Refiner also demonstrates stronger instruction-following ability for stress and pause control in targeted prosody modification. title: EmoSay: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Text-to-Emotional-Speech System for Affective Communication in Extended Reality Sikiru
abstract: ective Communication in Extended Reality Sikiru Ademola Adewale, Sunday D. Ubur, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Onyeka Emebo, Denis Gračanin While contemporary neural text-to-speech (TTS) systems have achieved high levels of intelligibility, they frequently lack the emotional nuance required for authentic affective communication. This limitation is particularly critical in Extended Reality (XR), where the absence of emotionally expressive audio can diminish user presence and spatial immersion. We present EmoSay, an Artificial Intelligence-driven Text-to-Emotional-Speech (TTES) system designed to bridge the semantic-affective gap in immersive environments. EmoSay modulates a neural synthesis pipeline using discrete emotional prompts, delivering the output through a Unity-based interface featuring high-fidelity spatialized audio. The system was evaluated through a comprehensive user study focusing on perception, engagement, and the subjective sense of empathy. Our results demonstrate that EmoSay significantly enhances the immersive experience, achieving a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 74.76, indicating strong usability and seamless integration within the XR workflow. Subjective assessments reveal a high degree of perceived naturalness and a strong positive correlation between emotional expressiveness and user engagement. Regression analysis identifies vocal naturalness as the strongest of the tested predictors of user satisfaction, suggesting that EmoSay's affective prosody helps meet the heightened expectations for realism in immersive settings. title: Speaking Longer Than Learned: Training-Free Long-Form Generation for Full-Stream Text-to-Speech
abstract: eung Lim, Jiseong Woo, Heeseung Kim Recent full-stream text-to-speech (TTS) models enable low-latency personalized synthesis as input text arrives. However, sustaining generation beyond the lengths seen during training without additional training remains largely unexplored. We systematically analyze VoXtream2, which extends generation by periodically discarding past context while retaining the acoustic prompt. We find that this strategy does not prevent degradation: pronunciation accuracy deteriorates near the end of the training range due to the range of positions in which the model operates rather than the loss of past context, while speaker similarity gradually declines throughout generation. Based on these findings, we propose two training-free modifications that reduce the attention window and strengthen attention to the acoustic prompt. Experiments show that these modifications preserve pronunciation accuracy and speaker similarity throughout long-form generation while retaining the naturalness of the original model. Ablations further show complementary effects of the two modifications. title: MIRA: Real-Time Full-Duplex Human-Robot Interaction for Embodied Companions
abstract: ction for Embodied Companions Lijian Lin, Ye Zhu, Fan Zhang, Yunfei Liu, Baofeng Li, Xianwen Zeng, Jianan Wang, Yu Li % !TEX root = ../main.tex Real-time embodied companion interaction requires a robot to infer user intent from streaming speech, generate timely responses, and execute expressive, interruptible motions. Existing systems typically decouple dialogue orchestration from gesture synthesis, relying on offline motion generation from complete audio. This separation leaves open how a deployed robot can dynamically synchronize response content, prosodic timing, and physical safety under incremental inputs and uncertain turn boundaries. We present MIRA, a unified framework for real-time full-duplex embodied companion interaction. Given streaming user speech, dialogue history, and vocal affect, MIRA predicts both the response text and an explicit embodiment cue that routes the response to the appropriate physical behavior. Discrete social behaviors (\eg listening and greeting) are mapped to validated robot trajectories, while speaking responses are accompanied by streaming, generative co-speech motion. For co-speech motion generation, we propose ROSCO, a prefix-conditioned diffusion model for streaming audio-to-joint motion generation. We further design RHPC, an inference scheme that maintains a sufficiently long temporal context for motion prediction while bounding physical commitment to a short, interruptible prefix. title: StreamTN: A Low-Latency Streaming Chinese Text Normalization Model for Streaming TTS in Dialogue Systems
abstract: alization Model for Streaming TTS in Dialogue Systems Wenhao Li, Jinrui Liang, Haoyu Zhang, Jingbin Hu, Xiaming Ren, Hanke Xie, Huakang Chen, Chengyou Wang, Dake Guo, Linhan Ma, Su Feng, Houdun Liu, Yunxiang Chen, Lei Xie Text-to-Speech (TTS) is an essential module that provides spoken responses in a spoken dialogue system (SDS) centered on a large language model (LLM). To ensure accurate TTS synthesis, responses generated by an LLM must be converted into TTS-readable formats via a Text Normalization (TN) module, imposing strict low-latency requirements in real-time SDS scenarios. Existing TN solutions are largely rule-based, rely on manual engineering, and generalize poorly to unseen patterns. Although an LLM itself can perform TN through prompt engineering, it faces key limitations: high first-token latency due to non-streaming processing, hallucination risks, and degraded intelligence or reasoning when the core LLM module is fine-tuned solely for TN. To address these challenges, we propose StreamTN, a lightweight LLM-based Chinese streaming TN model. Built on Qwen3-0.6B, StreamTN employs a dual-track streaming framework in which input tokens and output tokens are processed on two parallel tracks, enabling low-latency real-time inference without complex prompting. Moreover, task-specific fine-tuning yields superior TN performance and fewer hallucinations than rule-based systems and general-purpose LLMs. We also introduce a TN benchmark that spans diverse text scenarios, providing a comprehensive evaluation standard for speech generation in spoken dialogue systems. title: X-Pred MeanFlow for Streaming Token-to-Mel Speech Decoding
abstract: ecoding Hanke Xie, Xiaming Ren, Qirui Zhan, Jingbin Hu, Wenhao Li, Haoyu Zhang, Ruonan You, Chengyou Wang, Yunxiang Chen, Houdun Liu, Su Feng, Lei Xie Recent advancements in discrete token-based speech generation have highlighted the importance of efficient token-to-waveform synthesis in streaming and dialogue scenarios. Flow-matching acoustic decoders achieve high-quality token-to-mel generation, but their iterative sampling requires multiple neural function evaluations, limiting low-latency speech synthesis. MeanFlow reduces the sampling budget by modeling the average velocity over a temporal interval, yet maintaining high acoustic quality under extremely few-step token-to-mel generation remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose X-Pred MeanFlow, a few-step streaming token-to-mel decoder that reparameterizes MeanFlow with mel-space prediction. The decoder predicts a generalized mel field and analytically derives the corresponding average velocity for sampling, thereby preserving the MeanFlow formulation while providing a direct acoustic prediction target. We further introduce layer-selective block-wise attention to enable continuous chunk-wise generation with bounded context. Experiments show that X-Pred MeanFlow improves few-step token-to-mel synthesis over Direct-$u$ MeanFlow and supports stable streaming generation. title: Super Star: Towards Streaming Real-time Interactive Agents for Digital Humans
abstract: Wentao Jiang, Youchen Xie, Haidi Fan, Yajing Chen, Xin Wang, Ye Shi, Jingya Wang Existing co-speech gesture generation methods are predominantly studied in offline settings, where gestures are synthesized from complete speech segments. However, interactive digital humans in real-world scenarios are required to generate speech-synchronous gestures online, using only currently available response audio under strict latency constraints. As a result, prior methods are unsuitable for real-time interaction, as they either rely on future speech information or incur substantial inference delay. In this paper, we formulate online co-speech gesture generation for interactive digital humans and propose a real-time interactive framework that couples a streaming speech response module with an online gesture generation module. Specifically, the gesture generator is designed as a causal multimodal autoregressive model that predicts body motion from streaming response speech and motion history, enabling low-latency and speech-aligned gesture synthesis without access to future speech. To support this setting, we further propose an offline data synthesis pipeline tailored to virtual companion scenarios, which leverages topic- and emotion-aware subject corpora to construct diverse human-agent dialogues and then generates co-speech gestures conditioned on the agent responses. title: X2Streaming-TTS: Causal Token-Level Text-to-Speech from Streaming Text with Speech-State Inheritance
abstract: ch-State Inheritance Rime Wen, Zehan Liu, Shawn Qin, Lights Shi, Roy Gan, Hao Wang, Qian Wang Streaming text-to-speech is essential for low-latency spoken dialogue systems, yet many systems wait for sentence-level text and are therefore only pseudo-streaming. True token-level synthesis must generate speech from uncertain prefixes while maintaining perceptual continuity over an unbounded stream with bounded context. We present X2Streaming-TTS, a causal TTS framework that consumes asynchronously arriving text tokens and emits speech without accessing future input. To handle uncertain prefixes, we introduce causal commitment, which keeps ambiguous expressions provisional through uncertainty-aware buffering and performs capacity-adaptive, punctuation-aware segmentation. To preserve acoustic continuity, we further introduce causal speech-state inheritance, which carries the complete Code2Wav state and selected historical Talker states across segment boundaries. Together with an attention prior constraint, it blocks access to future positions while retaining bounded acoustic context. Experiments show that X2Streaming-TTS outperforms existing pseudo-streaming models on most subjective and objective metrics. Further analysis shows that causal commitment stabilizes online segmentation and reduces failures caused by insufficient context, while speech-state inheritance improves boundary continuity without degrading naturalness or speaker identity.
